mūla.devanāgarī: सर्वतः पाणि-पादं तत् सर्वतो ऽक्षि-शिरो-मुखम् | सर्वतः श्रुतिमल् लोके सर्वम् आवृत्य तिष्ठति
mūla.iast: sarvataḥ pāṇi-pādaṃ tat sarvato 'kṣi-śiro-mukham | sarvataḥ śrutimal loke sarvam āvṛtya tiṣṭhati
mūla.chapter_position: Chapter 13 (Kṣetra-Kṣetrajña-Vibhāga-Yoga (The Yoga of Distinction Between Field and Field-Knower)), verse 13
mūla.speaker: Krishna

senses_attested_in_panel.sense: इति। लोके यद् वस्तुजातं तत् सर्वं व्याप्य तिष्ठति परिशुद्धस्वरूपं देशादिपरिच्छेदरहिततया सर्वगतम् इत्यर्थः।।

advaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
advaita.divergence_note: Śaṅkara treats the all-sided limbs as borne by upādhi and mithyā, ascribed only figuratively (upacārataḥ) as marks of the knowable's existence; the verse is read as a deliberate adhyāropa to be withdrawn later. Contrast Rāmānuja, for whom the subject is the purified individual self with real all-sided capacity, and Śrīdhara, for whom the limbs display Brahman's acintya śakti rather than an unreal overlay.
advaita.english_rendering: That knowable has hands and feet on every side, eyes, heads and mouths on every side, hearing on every side, and it stands pervading everything in the world of beings. These hands and feet belong to the upādhi (limiting adjuncts) of the bodies of all creatures and are mithyā (unreal) as features of the kṣetrajña (knower of the field), yet they are imagined as if its attributes to establish that it exists, lest what was denied as 'neither sat nor asat' be taken for nothing. As the knowers of the tradition say: by adhyāropa (superimposition) and apavāda (rescission) the world-free is spoken of in worldly terms.

viśiṣṭādvaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
viśiṣṭādvaita.english_rendering: That pure form of the ātman (self) is capable of the work of hands and feet everywhere, and does the work of eye, head, mouth and ear everywhere. The Śruti says the supreme Brahman, though without hands and feet, speeds and grasps; the purified pratyagātman (individual self), by attaining sāmya (equality of nature) with Him, likewise does the work of hands and feet everywhere, as 'the knower, shaking off merit and demerit, stainless, reaches supreme equality' and 'having taken refuge in this knowledge they come to sādharmya (likeness of nature) with Me' declare. It stands pervading every thing in the world because, free of limitation by place and the like, its pure form reaches everywhere.
viśiṣṭādvaita.divergence_note: Sharpest divergence in the panel: for Rāmānuja 'tat' is not Brahman but the pariśuddha (purified) individual self, whose all-sided agency is real and established by śruti, gained by sāmya with Brahman (Muṇḍaka 3.1.3, Gītā 14.2). No upādhi, no mithyā; pervasion means absence of spatial limitation, not identity with all.

dvaita.divergence_note: ABSENT: the supplied Madhva text for this verse (his source_verse 13.14) reads only 'Sri Madhvacharya did not comment on this sloka.' No Dvaita bhāṣya exists to anchor a rendering; the English is the mūla only, not a Dvaita reading. Jayatīrtha's Prameyadīpikā is also silent on this verse.
dvaita.english_rendering: [No Madhva bhāṣya for this verse.] Mūla only: It has hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads and mouths everywhere, hearing everywhere in the world; it stands enveloping all.

śuddhādvaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
śuddhādvaita.english_rendering: Is it with form or formless? With form indeed: everywhere its hands and feet reach their ends, and the word anta (end) shows that in going and doing it shows itself delimited by its own will, while eyes, heads and mouths everywhere declare its primacy of knowing and its enjoyments. 'Hearing everywhere in the world' is said for the world of names, and 'it stands enveloping all' shows that such a one can take on delimitation; though these attributes become plain only after the world arises, they are stated first to proclaim that they are nitya (eternal).
śuddhādvaita.divergence_note: Vallabha reads the compound as 'sarvataḥ-pāṇi-pādāntam' and settles the sākāra / nirākāra question for sākāra: the limbs are real, eternal attributes of a Lord who delimits Himself by svecchā (own will). This rejects both Śaṅkara's mithyā overlay and Rāmānuja's transfer of the verse to the individual self.

bhakti.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
bhakti.divergence_note: Śrīdhara frames the verse as the first of five that answer an objection from 'sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma'; his key move is acintya śakti (Śvetāśvatara 6.8), so the all-sided limbs express a real power of Brahman, while still naming the limbs upādhi. Neither Śaṅkara's mithyā nor Rāmānuja's individual self.
bhakti.english_rendering: Lest Brahman, said to be beyond sat and asat, conflict with 'all this indeed is Brahman', the Lord shows its sarvātmatā (being the self of all) by its acintya śakti (inconceivable power), known from the Śruti as manifold and natural, as knowledge, strength and action, in five verses beginning here. Everywhere are its hands and feet, everywhere its eyes, heads and mouths; endowed with hearing everywhere, it stands in the world enveloping all. That is, through the hands and other upādhi (adjuncts) by which all beings act, it abides as the ground of all transaction.

advaita-bhakti.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
advaita-bhakti.divergence_note: Madhusūdana follows Śaṅkara's frame but builds an explicit inference: insentient activity requires a conscious overseer, so the knowable exists. He adds that the kṣetrajña is one in all bodies, not one per body, and that the relation to the world is adhyāsika, leaving Brahman untouched by it.
advaita-bhakti.english_rendering: Since the unconditioned Brahman is no object of the word or notion 'existent', a doubt arises that it is non-existent; to remove it at length, the Lord shows its existence through the instruments of all beings, as the conscious kṣetrajña (knower of the field) who sets in motion the insentient hands and feet in every body, for every activity of the insentient presupposes a conscious overseer. So of this knowable there can be no doubt of non-being. One, eternal and all-pervading, it envelops all that is insentient by its own being and shining through an adhyāsika (superimpositional) relation, and remains nirvikāra (changeless), not touched by an atom of the defects or merits of the inert world imposed on it.

vishishtadvaita.divergence_note: Ramanuja does not read 'na sat tan nasad' as an absolute negation of all predication; rather, Brahman transcends ordinary sat/asat because its nature as vishishta (qualified by cit and acit) exceeds the binary. Brahman is supremely real, not beyond reality.

shuddhadvaita.divergence_note: Vallabha diverges sharply from Shankara: Brahman is not nirvishesha (featureless) but svishesha (fully qualified) — the 'na sat na asat' formula is a floor, not a ceiling; it rules out finite categories while leaving Krishna's positive gunas intact.

so_what_questions: If the same capacity shows up in every pair of hands in my organization, where do I actually go to find it?
When I watch what people do, am I seeing what moves them, or only their hands?
Is it useful to describe something with pictures I know are not literally true, if that is the only way to point at it?
Does growing as a person give me real new reach, or only a better view of what was already there?
Is the power behind action located in the person acting, or does it simply work through them?
If something envelops everything, why do I experience myself as one small, separate point?

everyday_applications.advaita: When a founder says 'the company sees everything', the dashboards, managers and reports are borrowed eyes: useful for pointing at the attention behind them, false if taken as that attention. Use the description to locate what is really doing the seeing, then let the description go. A doctor reads the chart to find the patient, then puts the chart down.
everyday_applications.viśiṣṭādvaita: Rāmānuja's claim is that a cleaned-up self really gains reach; it is not an illusion. A teacher who has worked free of self-protection can actually attend to thirty students at once, in a way she could not when every remark was about her. The growth is real capacity, modeled on a greater one and earned by purification.
everyday_applications.dvaita: Madhva's bhāṣya is silent on this verse, so no Dvaita-specific application can be drawn from the supplied commentary; inventing one would put words in his mouth.
everyday_applications.śuddhādvaita: Vallabha insists the reach has a form and sets its own edges by choice. A parent who could be in every corner of a child's life chooses where their hand ends, and that chosen limit is part of the care, not a failure of it. Decide where your reach stops on purpose, instead of letting exhaustion decide for you.
everyday_applications.bhakti: Śrīdhara reads the many hands as one power working through everyone's ordinary work. A manager walking from the warehouse floor to the call center to accounts can see one capacity expressed in different jobs. That changes how credit is given and how blame is assigned.
everyday_applications.advaita-bhakti: Madhusūdana argues back from motion to a mover: tools move only because something aware drives them. When a project is running, ask what awareness is steering it, and notice that this awareness is not stained by the project's failures or flattered by its wins. A surgeon can lose a case without becoming the loss.

primary_meaning: It has hands and feet on every side, eyes and heads and mouths on every side, ears throughout the world, and it stands enveloping all.
